slides.headline: Caesar is dead. One man didn't move.
slides.sub: Jean-Léon Gérôme, The Death of Caesar, 1859-67

slides.headline: The Ides of March
slides.text: Rome, the Ides of March, 44 BC. In a Senate hall by the Theatre of Pompey, Julius Caesar has just been stabbed by senators.

slides.headline: Caesar
slides.text: There he lies, almost hidden under his toga, alone on the floor. The most powerful man in the world, abandoned.

slides.headline: The chair
slides.text: His chair is overturned. Follow the floor from it, and you can trace the last few steps he took before he fell.

slides.headline: The killers
slides.text: The killers walk away together, raising their blades in triumph. Gérôme paints the moment just after the murder, not the murder itself.

slides.headline: Panic
slides.text: A white cloak dropped on a bench, scrolls scattered on the floor. In the distance, others who had nothing to do with it are fleeing.

slides.headline: One man stays
slides.text: And far on the right, one senator is still sitting in his seat. Frozen with shock? Or quietly approving?

slides.headline: The petition
slides.text: On the floor lies a petition, beside a mosaic of Medusa's head. Legend says Caesar was handed a warning that morning, unread.

slides.headline: Freedom?
slides.text: The killers called it freedom. Instead it led to years of civil war and the end of the Republic. Heroes, or traitors?
